For every ε > 0 there is C(ε) such that for all X ≥ 2,
N(X) = #{1 ≤ n ≤ X : n is 2-full and n+1 is 3-full} ≤ C(ε) X^{3/10+ε}.

targets.statement: There is no integer n > 0 such that n is 2-full and n+1 is 3-full. Equivalently, for all cube-free k ≥ 1 and u ≥ 2 with rad(k) | u, k u³ − 1 is not powerful.

For every cube-free k ≥ 1 and every s ≥ 1 with k·s ≤ 10^5, the equation k u³ − s² t³ = 1 has no positive solution with rad(k) | u. Hence no solution n = s²t³ (with any t ≥ 1, and n of any size) has k·s ≤ 10^5. In particular, u³ − 1 = s²t³ has no solution with s ≤ 10^5 and any u.

There is an absolute δ > 0 such that for every cube-free k ≥ 1, the squarefree t ≤ T with gcd(t,k)=1 and rank E_{k,t}(Q) = 0 number at least δ·#{squarefree t ≤ T, gcd(t,k)=1} for T ≥ T₀(k). Every such fibre (k,t) contains no solution. Also give an explicit δ₁ for k = 1.
Every fibre (k,t) with k cube-free, t squarefree, gcd(k,t)=1 and k·t ≤ 10^4 contains no solution. That is, Y² = X³ − k²t³ has no integral point with X = ktu, Y = kt³s, s ≥ 1, rad(k) | u.
Assume Baker's explicit abc conjecture: c < (6/5)·r·(log r)^ω/ω!, where r = rad(abc) and ω = ω(abc). Then there is no n > 0 with n 2-full and n+1 3-full.
For every integer u ≥ 2, u³ − 1 is not powerful. This is the k = 1 case: n+1 is a perfect cube.

Here κ = 6·(ζ(3/2)/2ζ(3))·(c₃/3)·∏_p E_p, with explicit local correction factors E_p. For all integers k ≥ 2, n ≥ 0, m ≥ n+k: ∏_{i=1}^k (m+i) ≠ 4·∏_{i=1}^k (n+i). Hence the Lean statement erdos_686 is false, with witness N = 4.

The integer solutions of X³−X = 4(Y³−Y) are exactly {−1,0,1}² ∪ {±(3,2)}. Consequently F_3(m) = 4F_3(n) with m > n ≥ 0 only for (n,m) = (0,1). By the symmetry, 4 has no representation with k = 3, and none with m−n = 3.
For 2 ≤ t ≤ 100, t² is 3-representable (k = 3, m ≥ n+3) iff t ∈ {3, 4, 70}.

Let C₅: P(X) = 4P(Y), with P = x⁵−5x³+4x, X = m+3, Y = n+3, and ι(X,Y) = (−X,−Y). Let A = (1−ι)J(C₅), the 4-dimensional Prym. If rank A(Q) ≤ 3, then C₅(Q) = {−2,…,2}² ∪ {±(14/3, 11/3)}. Hence 4 is not 5-representable, and has no representation with m−n = 5.

Let k ≥ 3 be odd, α = 4^(1/k), c_k = (k²−1)(α⁻¹−α)/24, and X = m+(k+1)/2, Y = n+(k+1)/2 with F_k(m) = 4F_k(n) and Y ≥ k². - Then |Y(X−αY) − c_k| ≤ C·k⁴/Y² for an explicit absolute C. - Hence, with p/q = X/Y in lowest terms, (p,q) = (r·p_{j+1} ± s·p_j, r·q_{j+1} ± s·q_j) for convergents p_j/q_j of α and integers r, s ≥ 0 with rs < 2|c_k|+1 ≈ 0.23k. This is Worley's theorem.

For every q ≥ 2, k ≥ 2, n ≥ 0, m ≥ n+k: if N = ∏(q^{m+i}−1)/∏(q^{n+i}−1) is an integer, then N has at least k−1 distinct prime factors ≡ 1 (mod m+i). In particular no N ≤ 2^{k} and no power of 2 is q-representable.
The anti-invariant class [P − ιP] with P = (14/3, 11/3) ∈ C₅(Q) has infinite order. Hence rank J(C₅)(Q) ≥ 6 = genus, and classical Chabauty–Coleman on C₅ cannot work.

Write F_k(a) = (a+1)⋯(a+k). For all n ≥ 0 and k, d ≥ 1, F_k(n+d)/F_k(n) = F_d(n+k)/F_d(n). Hence: - 4 is not representable ⇐ [for every a ∈ A and every b ≥ a, F_a(n+b) ≠ 4F_a(n)], where A = {odd a ≥ 3} ∪ {even a ≥ 342}. This uses the harness even-k result, which covers all gaps. - In that remaining case, s ≥ max(a³/10⁴, a·b/ln 4·(1−o(1))).
